historyReviewBoundary: All 115 histories have author source checks. Final independent review covered metadata and numerical checks for all 115 classes, 12 deeper class targets and source-gap samples in seven classes. It did not independently verify every passage of every cited source.

history.name: Hydrazinophthalazine direct arteriolar vasodilators

starting.description: According to Sneader, a blood-pressure fall and peripheral dilation were observed during Ciba's synthetic imidazoline investigations; the laboratory expanded to other nitrogen heterocycles and hypotensive screening of phthalazines yielded hydralazine, though why it expanded is not expressly stated. Chast instead directly reports diversion after a hypotensive effect appeared in an antimalarial search. Both are retrospective accounts; the primary evidence read here does not resolve the initial program.

inspiration.description: Chast directly attributes the change to a hypertension application to hydralazine's observed effect during an antimalarial search. Sneader describes an earlier blood-pressure/peripheral-vascular effect of synthetic imidazolines, followed by expanded screening that yielded hydralazine, but does not expressly identify the reason for expansion. This classification uses Ha's broad biological-inspiration definition and does not imply a natural-source scaffold.

steps.description: A historical review describes blood-pressure lowering in an imidazoline series, followed by exploration of other nitrogen heterocycles and hypotensive screening of phthalazines.

Chast's historical account directly links hydralazine's observed circulatory effect during an antimalarial search to its application for hypertension; the upstream purpose differs from Sneader's account.

In their 1949 patent the inventors described a preparation of 1-hydrazinophthalazine and claimed pressure-lowering effects for their compounds; the 1950 original report described the pharmacological properties of substituted phthalazines.
The 1951 chemistry abstract describes modification of the ring system and hydrazine group in related compounds, without establishing a particular optimization sequence.

A 1952 clinical study measured cardiovascular and renal effects of the named compound and interpreted its hemodynamic action as peripheral vascular relaxation, while the site of action remained uncertain.

design.description: Ciba researchers screened related phthalazine structures and identified hydralazine as a long-acting peripheral dilator according to a later history; the inventors' patent describes chemical synthesis. The 1951 chemistry abstract describes ring and hydrazine-group substitutions. A specific causal optimization sequence or superiority of individual alterations is not established by the material read.

circumstances.description: The historical review describes screening the phthalazine series for hypotensive activity; this does not settle whether the original effect or the initial synthesis was unexpected.

limits: Hydralazine is the sole cohort member; this is the hydrazinophthalazine founding history, not the heterogeneous set of all vasodilators.

The competing narratives concern the same hydralazine research lineage, not established separate founding branches; observation-led does not assert which upstream program is correct or that a natural scaffold was used.
conflicts: Sneader describes an imidazoline-related heterocycle and hypotensive-screening program; Chast and the earlier Dustan review describe an antimalarial-search origin. Their relationship is unestablished. Chast and Dustan use the same wording and are not independent corroboration; the accessible Reubi report cited by Dustan does not establish an antimalarial starting program.
gaps: Pages 19–20 of the 1950 original pharmacology report were not accessible; the visible final page does not identify the tested hydralazine compound or originating program.
Druey and Ringier 1951 was read only as an indexed abstract; Druey and Marxer's 1959 inventor-authored article was located but not read, so its contents and account type are unknown.

Schroeder 1952, cited for the antimalarial-origin anecdote, was not accessible; its ability to support that anecdote is unknown. Its author initials/title differ between PubMed and other bibliographic sources.
The earlier patent application/file history was not inspected; the issued 1949 patent does not by itself establish the timing of each discovery step.
